target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: A second holding-house case a month later, this time with no arrest.

claim: The officer-in-charge of Teknaf police station said in December 2024 that every winter broker rings hold Rohingya from the Ukhiya and Teknaf camps for ransom in the name of sending them to Malaysia by sea, and that sometimes they put them on a big trawler, sail around for several days, leave them in different parts of Cox's Bazar and run off with the money.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: A police officer describing the fake voyage as a routine trick.

claim: According to police and local representatives in Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, trafficking by sea rose again from January 2024 after six or seven years of being largely stopped, and in the past year (to January 2025) law enforcers rescued at least 600 people, including 45 traffickers, in eight or nine operations on the Teknaf coast, most of those rescued being Rohingya men, women and children.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Dates the revival of the Teknaf boat route to January 2024 and gives a one-year rescue count.

claim: Rafiq Ullah, a Rohingya leader at the Lambashia camp in Ukhiya, told Prothom Alo in January 2025 that more than five hundred young men and women of marriageable age had been sent towards Malaysia from that camp in the past year and that more than three hundred had been caught by law enforcers and come back.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Scale from a single camp, and the share caught.

claim: Kamal Hossain, a Rohingya leader at the Balukhali camp, said in January 2025 that before reaching Malaysia Rohingya are held at the Thailand or Myanmar border while ransom is demanded from their relatives in the camps in Bangladesh, and that if this fails there are attempts to abduct members of that family.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: The ransom stage en route and what happens to the family at home if it is not paid.

claim: Police and local representatives said at least 193 people, 86 of them Rohingya, were abducted in Teknaf in a little over a year to January 2025 and at least 98 were freed on ransom; the district's additional superintendent of police said investigations of several of the abductions found a link to human trafficking and the involvement of some local residents of Teknaf.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Abduction for ransom around the Teknaf departure points, tied by police to trafficking.

claim: Prothom Alo reported in January 2025 that 20 abduction cases had been filed at Teknaf police station in the past year, and the station's officer-in-charge said that although releases on ransom are reported in the media, none of the victims wants to come to the station to complain or give information.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Why few cases follow: victims who paid ransom do not complain.

claim: According to an ISPR (armed forces' public relations) statement, on 8 April 2025 the navy ship Durjoy seized the fishing trawler FB Kulsuma in the Bay of Bengal 44 nautical miles south-west of St Martin's island with 214 passengers, 118 men, 68 women and 28 children, who were being sent illegally to Malaysia; the trawler had set out at about 2 a.m. after 7 April from Shaplapur beach in Baharchhara union, Teknaf, and had no minimum life-saving equipment or adequate food and water.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: A dated 2025 boat interception: boats still leave Teknaf, with over 200 aboard a fishing trawler.

claim: A sub-inspector of the Shah Porir Dwip police outpost, citing the Rohingya rescued in April 2025, said several broker rings were active in stages, bringing people out of the camps, driving them to the Kachchhapia area of Teknaf and putting them on the trawler, which was to pass the St Martin's coast and reach Thailand through Myanmar waters, from where the passengers were promised they would be handed on and delivered to Malaysia.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: The sea route step by step in 2025: camp, vehicle to Kachchhapia, trawler, Myanmar waters, Thailand, handover.

claim: The Shah Porir Dwip police sub-inspector said the Rohingya rescued in April 2025 had been promised good jobs in Malaysia or marriage to a suitable man, that many girls had been married over the phone, and that the broker rings had taken Tk 30,000 to 50,000 from most of them.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: The 2025 price and the phone-marriage lure.

claim: A driver from Kotbazar, Ukhiya, rescued from the trawler seized in April 2025 said two men hired his auto-rickshaw on 2 April, held him at gunpoint in a deserted spot and took him to the Kachchhapia hills in Baharchhara, Teknaf, where he was kept for four days in a hut with 20 to 25 other men and women, and that he was forced onto the trawler on the night of 7 April.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: A Bangladeshi abducted and forced onto the boat.

claim: After the April 2025 interception the 214 passengers were handed to Teknaf police on 9 April; the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner said legal action was being taken against 12 of the rescued Rohingya for involvement in various crimes and the rest were handed back to the camps.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: What the authorities did with those intercepted.

claim: At a roundtable on sea journeys abroad organised by BRAC and Prothom Alo in Cox's Bazar (reported by Prothom Alo on 6 June 2026), Bangladesh Coast Guard East Zone (Chattogram) zonal commander Captain Mohammad Mizanur Rahman said Cox's Bazar is one route for sea journeys abroad: people brought from different parts of the country are kept in the hills and other places there, taken in small boats to a large trawler or ship when the moment suits, and the torture begins once they are on board.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: The section describes only the Cambodia-Thailand land route and the 2012-15 boats; this gives the 2026 mechanics of the Cox's Bazar sea departure (hill hideouts, small boats to a trawler) from a named official, and answers part of the section's Need to know on whether boats still leave.

claim: Tarekur Rahman of Maheshkhali, Cox's Bazar, who came back from the Malaysia route, told the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that a broker put him on a ship with talk of a good job in Malaysia, took him to Myanmar and took Tk 1 lakh from his family, then took Tk 7 lakh more in Thailand, and that he was caught at the border on the way to Malaysia, served a jail term and came home.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: A named survivor case of the sea route with the amounts taken at each stage. Note: the fuller transcript (article 533a06e4) gives his account differently (held and jailed in Myanmar for about seven months, no Thailand stage); the two versions should be reconciled before use.

claim: Aung Aung U Jewel told the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that brokers caught him while he was a college student with an offer to take him to Australia by way of Malaysia for Tk 12 lakh, took him first from Cox's Bazar to Myanmar, where police arrested him and he was jailed, and that he later came home with the embassy's help.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: A second named case: the "Australia via Malaysia" pitch, its price (Tk 12 lakh) and the fact that the journey ended in a Myanmar jail, none of which the section has.

claim: Suraiya Akter Sweety, a deputy secretary and camp-in-charge at the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commission, said at the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that the tendency to go abroad by sea is high among Rohingya as well as Bangladeshis, especially teenage girls, who are taken by sea to Malaysia and Indonesia with the lure of a "better husband", and that many women are trafficked this way.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: The section has no account of how girls and women are recruited for the boats; this is the marriage lure, from a named camp official.

claim: Citing accounts given by victims and families who come to the ministry, the state minister for expatriates' welfare, Md Nurul Haque, said at the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that on illegal sea journeys brokers hold people hostage and extract large sums from their families, do not give them even minimal food and water, many die on the way, and those who reach a shore are detained by police there.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: An official statement of what happens on the boats (hostage-taking for ransom, no food or water, deaths, arrest on landing); the section's "What happens" covers only arrests on the land route. The minister was speaking of sea routes generally, not Malaysia alone.

claim: Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC's Migration Programme said at the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that the dead found in the mass graves discovered in Thailand and Malaysia in 2015 had no names or identities and their graves were marked only with numbers.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
placement: other: The path (the older boat route)
why_new: The section mentions the 2015 mass graves but not that the bodies were never identified and the graves carry numbers only.

claim: The Deputy Commissioner of Cox's Bazar, Md A Mannan, said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that the sea off Cox's Bazar is calm in winter, so the risk of trafficking by sea rises then.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Gives the season of the boat departures, which the section lacks.

claim: The Deputy Commissioner of Cox's Bazar said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that families who lose a member on a sea journey abroad, or are cheated, often do not want to admit what happened, which makes it hard to investigate the crime and identify the offenders.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Explains, from the district administration, why boat cases go uninvestigated; not in the section.

claim: The Coast Guard's East Zone commander said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that traffickers bring people from around the country to hilly areas and try to send them out by sea in the dark of night, and that Bangladesh's coastline is 710 km long and a boat can be launched from any point on it.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Adds night departures and that launches are not tied to one landing point; complements MY2-1 from the fuller transcript.

claim: The Coast Guard's East Zone commander said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that on the trafficking boats there is no food, clean water or toilet, that deaths happen and the bodies are thrown into the sea.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Conditions on the boats and the disposal of bodies at sea, stated by the Coast Guard; not in the section.

claim: The Coast Guard's East Zone commander said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that even when cases are filed against traffickers, in many instances they get out of jail and go back to the same work.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: What does not happen after a case is filed: the section's "The law" covers only Malaysian and Thai law, nothing on outcomes in Bangladesh.

claim: The Superintendent of Police of Cox's Bazar, A N M Sajedur Rahman, said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that traffickers there build friendships through social media, invite people to come for a visit and then abduct or traffic them, and that some fishermen think they can earn more by trafficking people than by fishing.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Two mechanisms the section lacks: the social-media friendship and "come for a visit" lure that ends in abduction, and fishermen as the boat crews.

claim: Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC, who reported as a journalist on sea trafficking and the Thailand-Malaysia border mass graves between 2012 and 2015, said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that about one lakh people were trafficked in that period, and that in 2015 rescued Bangladeshis, many of them teenagers, were sent home with their hands and feet in chains.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
placement: other: The path (the older boat route)
why_new: The section says "thousands" tried the boats in 2012-15; this gives an eyewitness estimate of about one lakh and how the rescued were returned.

claim: Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that about two lakh people have crossed the Bay of Bengal in the past decade and many have gone missing, and that although brokers promise Malaysia or Australia, many are tortured and ransom is extracted.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: The section has no figure for the Bay of Bengal route; he gives no source for the figure.

claim: Astrid Castelein, UNHCR's assistant representative (protection), said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that in 2023 alone about 5,787 people went missing during illegal sea journeys abroad, about 25% of them women and children, and that half of the missing were Rohingya and half Bangladeshi citizens.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: A UNHCR figure for the sea route. Caution: the transcript's numbers look garbled (the next sentence gives 39% women and 50% children for the same group); check against UNHCR's own publication before using.

claim: Tarekur Rahman told the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that a broker, promising an easy Malaysian visa, trafficked him and others from Maheshkhali to Myanmar, where they were beaten, Tk 1 lakh was taken from the family and they were moved to another hidden place, tortured and threatened with death.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: First-person account of the ransom stage in Myanmar; the section has no survivor account of the sea route.

claim: Tarekur Rahman said that under torture his family was forced to sell their house to pay the traffickers, that even then food sometimes came only after three or four days, and that after taking another large sum on a false promise of sending them to Malaysia the traffickers took them towards the border, where they were caught and held in a Myanmar prison for about seven months.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: How the money keeps being extracted (house sold, second payment for the "onward" leg) and where it ended: seven months in a Myanmar prison. Differs from the news report of the same event (article 300ce3de), which has a Tk 7 lakh payment in Thailand.

claim: Tarekur Rahman said that while he was in the Myanmar prison he and the others got no real help from the Bangladesh embassy, and that they finally got home on money sent by their families.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Evidence of what the embassy route delivered in practice for one detainee in Myanmar (nothing, by his account); the section lists only embassy contacts. Aung Aung U Jewel, at the same event, said he returned with embassy help.

claim: Aung Aung U Jewel told the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that he could not afford the language tests needed to go legally, so he set off when brokers promised an easy, cheap route to Australia by way of Malaysia; he later realised they had entered Myanmar, and after several days walking over hills they were detained, and he spent a month on remand and several months in prison.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Why he took the route (the cost of the legal one) and that the "Malaysia" leg was in fact an overland walk into Myanmar; fuller than the news report's version.

claim: Aung Aung U Jewel said he had no contact with his family while detained in Myanmar, managed to send a letter to his mother through a Myanmar police officer, and later learned that the brokers had also taken money from his family as the cost of rescuing him.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: A second charge by the same brokers: money taken from the family as a "rescue cost" while the man sat in a foreign prison. Also relevant to "People who offer to get your money back".

claim: Aung Aung U Jewel said that when fighting began while he was held in Thandwe prison in Myanmar, the prisoners were moved elsewhere and forced to do various work, and that he later returned home with the help of the Bangladesh embassy.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: Names the prison (Thandwe) and what happened to detainees when the fighting reached it; shows the embassy did arrange this return.

claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that many Bangladeshis and Rohingya are trying to go to Malaysia across the Bay of Bengal, and that reports of the deaths of about 500 Rohingya had come in the previous week.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: The section treats the boat route as the 'older route' (2012-15) and asks whether boats still leave; BRAC said in July 2026 that Bangladeshis and Rohingya are attempting the Bay of Bengal crossing now. He gave no source or place for the 500 deaths.

claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that many people who are in Malaysia are being drawn into a trap of fraud with assurances that they will be sent on to Australia.
target_section: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
why_new: A new onward-migration fraud aimed at Bangladeshis already in Malaysia (Australia promised); not in the guide.

claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2025 that women have also been lured into a love affair, married and taken to India with a child and then forced into sex work; one woman said her six-month-old child was held hostage and dangled from a balcony with a threat to drop the child if she did not obey.
target_section: Marriage, family-visa and fake-nikahnama schemes
why_new: Marriage used for trafficking to India, with a child as hostage; the section covers China only.

claim: A Rohingya young woman from the Balukhali camp (Camp 9) in Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, was married over the phone on 3 April 2025 to a young man living in Malaysia whom she had never met, her parents having agreed at a broker's word; on 5 April she was handed to a broker, kept with other Rohingya women in a house in the Kachchhapia hills of Teknaf and put on a trawler for Malaysia that the navy seized on 8 April, and she said her family had spent about Tk 50,000 by the time she boarded.
target_section: Marriage, family-visa and fake-nikahnama schemes
why_new: A phone marriage to an unseen husband used to put a woman on a smuggling boat; the section has only China cases.

claim: On the night of Monday 26 May 2025 the Airport Armed Police Battalion (APBn) arrested two Chinese nationals, Hu Junjun (30) and Zhang Leiji (54), and a Bangladeshi, Md Nayan Ali (30), in Bashundhara Residential Area, Dhaka, on charges of human trafficking, after a 19-year-old woman being taken through Shahjalal airport complained to the APBn at the roundabout by the airport's main entrance that the two Chinese men were trying to traffic her to China.
target_section: Marriage, family-visa and fake-nikahnama schemes
why_new: A 2025 China marriage case stopped at the airport by the woman's own verbal complaint, with where she complained.

claim: According to the APBn's press release of 28 May 2025, the two Chinese nationals had come to Bangladesh a year earlier, lived in Bashundhara and built ties with dalals around the country; with Nayan Ali's help the woman was persuaded by threats and inducements to marry, a passport and other papers were made in her name at a false address, and she was married to Hu Junjun in March 2025 with a denmohar (dower) of Tk 10 lakh.
target_section: Marriage, family-visa and fake-nikahnama schemes
why_new: Steps the section lacks: the foreigners settle in Dhaka first, work through local dalals, and get a passport made at a false address.

claim: The APBn said Zhang Leiji bought an air ticket in the woman's name to take her to China without telling her, and the arrested men took her by force from the house to Shahjalal airport.
target_section: Marriage, family-visa and fake-nikahnama schemes
why_new: The ticket bought without the bride's knowledge.

claim: From questioning the accused and from the woman's information the APBn confirmed that more local and foreign traffickers and women victims were in a house in Bashundhara Residential Area; a raid there arrested Nayan Ali, the others fled, and the police said they recovered important evidence and had initial proof that the ring had long been involved in trafficking.
target_section: Marriage, family-visa and fake-nikahnama schemes
why_new: A holding house in Dhaka with other women.

claim: On 28 May 2025 the woman's mother filed a case at Airport police station under sections 6(1), 6(2), 7, 8 and 10 of the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012.
target_section: Marriage, family-visa and fake-nikahnama schemes
why_new: Which sections were used and that a parent was the complainant.

claim: The Airport APBn's superintendent of police (operations), Mohammad Mozammel Haque, said in May 2025 that this was the second recent detention of Chinese nationals for trafficking at Shahjalal airport, and that some rings, with the help of local dalals, target women from simple, poor village families and try to traffic them to China with various inducements.
target_section: Marriage, family-visa and fake-nikahnama schemes
why_new: A named police officer on who is targeted and that it was the second such airport case.

claim: A 28-year-old woman from Savar who was told she would be sent to Canada was trafficked to Nadia district in West Bengal, India, and came home after seven months in a jail there, Prothom Alo reported in January 2024.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: A Canada promise that ended in an Indian jail; no India case in the guide.

claim: A ring trafficked women to India in the name of TikTok; one young woman escaped from India to Bangladesh on 7 May 2021 and on 1 June filed a case at Hatirjheel police station naming 12 people, and Rifadul Islam alias Hridoy (26), known as 'TikTok Hridoy', was involved in trafficking her.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: TikTok as the bait for trafficking to India; not in the guide.

claim: Prothom Alo reported in January 2024 that three years on, the investigation of the TikTok trafficking case filed at Hatirjheel police station was not finished, although accused arrested in India over the same incident had already been tried and punished there; Salma Ali of BNWLA said the lack of accountability of those investigating is why accused are not properly punished.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: Same crime: punished in India, still under investigation in Bangladesh.

claim: A 22-year-old woman living near the border in Jashore, about 30 km from Jashore town, told Prothom Alo in February 2025 that she was taken to India on the promise of a job and sold to a brothel, that Indian police rescued her two years later and she was sent back to Bangladesh, and that she saw three Bangladeshi girls in the brothel; BNWLA rehabilitated her after the rescue.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: A first-hand account of the job promise ending in an Indian brothel.

claim: Justice and Care, an organisation that works against trafficking, said the return of at least 10 women and girls trafficked across the border in the seven months from August 2024 to February 2025 was in process; Indian police had rescued them from brothels in Hyderabad, Maharashtra and Bengaluru.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: Where in India the women end up.

claim: By the count of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), 145 people, traffickers included, were detained while being trafficked illegally from August 2024 to January 2025, 55 of them women and children, and 162 people were repatriated from India in the same period.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: Official border counts.

claim: Three girls in class eight at a Dhaka school said that in January 2025 one of them received a message from a Facebook ID named 'Nil Pakhi' saying 'Will you go to India to learn dance? Tk 50,000 a month salary'; the ID belonged to a girl of the same age whom she already knew, the girl's mother used the same ID, and that mother helped the three set off for India.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: The exact bait message and that it came from a known peer's account.

claim: The three girls said they boarded a bus from Dhaka to Jhenaidah on the morning of 10 February 2025; the bus conductor handed them to a man in Jhenaidah, who took them to a woman's house; in the evening they were put on a battery-run auto-rickshaw whose driver handed them to a man in the border area of Maheshpur.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: The relay of handlers, step by step.

claim: BGB members chased the three girls and the man taking them across the border at Maheshpur, Jhenaidah, on 10 February 2025; one girl tripped and fell, the BGB rescued all three, and the man, who had a gamcha (cotton towel) tied over his face, escaped.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: How the attempt was stopped.

claim: One of the three girls filed a case at Maheshpur police station on 24 February 2025 under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012; no one had been arrested in the case when Prothom Alo reported on 8 March 2025.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: Outcome: case filed, no arrest.

claim: A 22-year-old divorced woman in Dhaka with cancer, whose treatment was costing a lot, was told by a woman neighbour that treatment is cheaper in India and that she could work there and pay for it herself; she was trafficked to India on 10 October 2024, and Hyderabad police rescued her from a brothel on 21 November.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: Cheap medical treatment as the bait, offered by a neighbour.

claim: A 15-year-old girl from a poor family wanted to go to India for work on the word of a cousin whom relatives believed to be a domestic worker in Maharashtra; she was trafficked on 11 February 2025, Maharashtra police rescued her on 23 February, and a Justice and Care programme officer said the girl had been used for sex work.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: A relative already in India as the recruiter.

claim: People concerned told Prothom Alo in early 2025 that trafficking to India goes through Putkhali, Daulatpur, Gatipara, Sadipur and Rudrapur around Benapole in Jashore, through Maheshpur in Jhenaidah and through the Satkhira border, with scattered cases through Tamabil in Sylhet and the Cumilla border.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: The named crossing points.

claim: Binoy Krishna Mallick, executive director of Rights Jashore, said in early 2025 that traffickers now take Tk 15,000 to 20,000 per person just for getting someone across the border, far more than before, because checks have tightened; rescued women said that in the brothels they were told they had been bought for Tk 2 to 3 lakh.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
placement: The contract price and the final price
why_new: The crossing fee and the price a woman is told she was sold for.

claim: When someone trafficked from Bangladesh is rescued in India, the Indian Border Security Force (BSF) hands the person over to the BGB and immigration police at the 'zero line' of the Benapole border.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: How and where a rescued woman is handed back.

claim: Lt Col Saifullah Siddiqui, commander of the 49 Border Guard Battalion in Jashore, told Prothom Alo that each person in the trafficking process has a separate task, so the victims themselves cannot say who took them from which place.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: Why victims cannot name the chain; from a named BGB commander.

claim: Justice and Care's count of victims the BGB placed in its custody shows that in the 14 months from January 2024 to February 2025, 186 women and children were brought back across the Bangladesh-India border and 133 were rescued at the border; of these, between August 2024 and February 2025, 87 were brought back from India and 88 were rescued while being trafficked; the figures cover only the Jhenaidah, Chuadanga and Jashore areas.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: NGO count with its coverage limit stated.

claim: A UN global report on human trafficking published in 2024 said 452 women (228 of them trafficked abroad) and 63 girls were trafficked from Bangladesh from April 2023 to March 2024, more than in earlier years.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: UN count of women and girls.

claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2025 that traffickers usually target women from low-income families who are in financial trouble.
target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
why_new: Who is targeted.

claim: Fatema Akter said that her age has gone up and her passport also shows a higher age, and that despite many attempts she can no longer go abroad.
target_section: The agent wants to change my age on the passport. Is that a problem?
why_new: A returnee blocked from going again by the age shown on her passport.

claim: The assistant director of the Cox's Bazar regional passport office said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that some people first get a passport with wrong information and later try to change it, that under a February 2025 circular the national ID data is the basis of the passport, and that responsibility for any mismatch lies with the person concerned.
target_section: The agent wants to change my age on the passport. Is that a problem?
why_new: Adds the February 2025 circular and who bears the consequence of wrong passport data: the holder, not the agent who arranged it.

claim: A 34-year-old Narayanganj woman went to Saudi Arabia in July 2022 after being told she would do housework for Tk 30,000 a month, and was physically and mentally abused there; her husband said the people who had sent her demanded Tk 3 lakh 20 thousand to bring her back, and that she was put out of the house after threatening suicide and then came home.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: A demand for money from the senders to bring an abused domestic worker home; the section has no such mechanism.

claim: The Narayanganj woman's husband said he filed a case at Hatirjheel police station on 24 November 2022 naming three men as traffickers; in January 2024 the police investigation was still unfinished, and the investigating sub-inspector said he had written to several institutions for information and had not received it.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: Outcome: more than a year on, no charge sheet.

claim: BRAC's Migration Programme said in January 2024 that women who go to Saudi Arabia as domestic workers keep coming home after abuse by employers, that some who were sexually abused return pregnant, and that women domestic workers are forced to return from Saudi Arabia almost every month.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: BRAC on the pattern of returns; the section has cases but no statement of how regular it is.

claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 16 January 2024 said there is almost no example of action being taken against the accused recruiting agencies after women workers come back empty-handed and abused.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: What did not happen to agencies; it is the newspaper's own assessment and should be attributed as such.

claim: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare's February 2025 notice stated that under the existing memorandum of understanding between Bangladesh and Malaysia there is no scope for women workers to be employed in Malaysia.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: A ministry statement that any Malaysia job offer to a woman worker falls outside the agreement; not found in the scam or illegal-routes chapters.

claim: A Satkhira woman went to Saudi Arabia on 21 November 2024 after being told she would work as a cleaner; she was given domestic work in a house, said she was sexually abused there, and came back in January 2025.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: A cleaner job that turned into domestic work, with dates.

claim: The Satkhira woman filed a case in a Satkhira court on 16 February 2025; Monirul Islam, owner of Lamim Visa Care in Satkhira, was arrested in the case, while another accused, Md Rafiqul Islam, owner of M/s Siam Trade International in Dhaka, told Prothom Alo on 4 March that she came back because she was already ill and could not work.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: A court case leading to an arrest of a local visa-office owner, and the Dhaka firm's denial.

claim: On 3 July 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission filed a case against four BMET officials and the owners and officials of five agencies on a charge of trafficking women abroad on forged papers; it said its raid on BMET's Dhaka office on 29 May found proof of the ring's irregularities, and it alleges that applications were filed with another woman's passport number in place of the real applicant's and approved for clearance without a check against BMET's database.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: This section's cases do not include the ACC case, which the ACC itself frames as trafficking of women with officials' help; it is in the guide only under BMET clearance.

claim: A 2025 study by Badabon Sangha, an organisation working on women migrant workers' rights, in Dhaka, Manikganj, Gopalganj, Sunamganj, Narsingdi, Cumilla and Pabna found that 27.6 percent of women migrated without having any source of income, which its programme manager Fariha Jesmin said points to forced migration; she said many took high-interest loans or sold assets, and that abroad they face low pay, loss of control of their passports, long hours and abuse.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: A survey figure on distress migration by women, with the debt and passport-control pattern.

claim: Naznin Akter, a Bangladeshi woman who returned from Malaysia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that she separated from her husband five years ago, was struggling to support two children and decided to go to Malaysia to get free of debt; an acquaintance offered her restaurant work at about BDT 60 thousand a month, and she had to pay more than BDT 2.5 lakh to go, which she raised by selling jewellery and borrowing.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: A named 2025 Malaysia case of a woman (restaurant job, wage promised, sum paid, how raised); the section's cases are Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Dubai and Cambodia.

claim: Naznin Akter, a Bangladeshi woman who returned from Malaysia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that in Malaysia her family was also pressed for money, she was kept in a hotel and then moved to a closed room where she was held for six days in a row and tortured only for asking where she was, and that she managed to come home on 21 November through her brothers' efforts.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: Completes the case: confinement, pressure on the family, and return within a week through her brothers, with no mention of any help from authorities.

claim: Shariful Hasan, associate director of BRAC, said in July 2026 that trafficking used to be done by force but is now done mainly in the name of migration, with people lured through job advertisements, and that traffickers do not get exemplary punishment.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: A named expert's description of the shift from forced trafficking to trafficking through migration offers.

claim: Professor Tasneem Siddiqui of RMMRU said on 30 July 2026 that, because of various kinds of fraud, the number of women migrating fell by about 41% in 2025 compared with 2022.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: A trend figure for women's migration with the cause RMMRU attributes it to; the section has only CID case counts.

claim: In a letter to BMET on 23 July 2026 seeking information on 57 agencies, the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) said it had filed a case in June 2025 against five agencies for acquiring illegal wealth by trafficking women abroad with forged papers made in collusion with dishonest BMET officials, and that the investigation had found allegations against 52 more agencies.
target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
why_new: The cross-country guide has no ACC case on trafficking women; this one alleges forged papers made with BMET officials' collusion and covers 57 agencies. The Malaysia doc already uses it for three listed agencies.

claim: Officials of several government bodies told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that most women who leave a Saudi household before the two-year contract ends run away and take shelter in the embassy's safe home, from where they are sent to the Saudi government's safe home, and the Saudi government pays for sending them home; if a woman wants to return within three months of arriving, her return is arranged through the Saudi company that recruited her.
target_section: What if I'm abused? Where can I go?
why_new: The actual path home (embassy safe home, then Saudi government safe home, who pays, the three-month rule); the FAQ only says safe homes exist.

claim: Lutfa Begum of Brahmanbaria went to Saudi Arabia as a domestic worker in March 2020 and worked 1 month 5 days; she told Prothom Alo she had to work in two neighbouring houses and the men of the house behaved badly, that she asked the person who had sent her for work elsewhere and did not get it, and that when she asked to go home she was sent to a shelter, where she stayed about three months before returning.
target_section: What if I'm abused? Where can I go?
why_new: A named account of work in two houses and three months in a safe home.

claim: Lutfa Begum said she was paid no wages for her work in Saudi Arabia in 2020, and that after coming home she received Tk 30,000 in cash assistance in two instalments.
target_section: What if I'm abused? Where can I go?
why_new: What a returnee actually received (Tk 30,000, source of the money not stated in the article).

claim: The Cumilla manpower office's assistant director said there is almost no psychological counselling service for migrant workers, especially women workers.
target_section: What if I'm abused? Where can I go?
why_new: What is not available at district level.

claim: People in the migration sector told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that training before a woman is sent to Saudi Arabia is compulsory but is not followed in some cases, and that the quality of the training is also questioned.
target_section: What is the housekeeping course?
why_new: The compulsory course is sometimes skipped.

claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 16 January 2024 said many women back from Saudi Arabia say the roughly month-long training given before departure is not enough, that some cannot read or write and many cannot sign their name and can only give a thumbprint, and that the language of the country they go to is unknown to them.
target_section: What is the housekeeping course?
why_new: Returnees on the length of the course, and that many sign contracts by thumbprint.

claim: Kamruzzaman, principal of the Cumilla Technical Training Centre, said in April 2026 that attendance at women workers' training is now monitored online, and that the policy requirement that agencies take at least 10% trained workers must be enforced.
target_section: What is the housekeeping course?
why_new: Online attendance monitoring answers the earlier complaint that the course is skipped.

claim: A T M Mahbubul Karim, joint secretary and project director of the RAISE project, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that domestic work abroad is not the same as at home, and that working in 50-degree heat, cooking local food and using modern appliances need training.
target_section: What is the housekeeping course?
placement: other: official on why training is needed
why_new: A government official's concrete description of what differs in domestic work abroad.

claim: Jasiya Khatun, director of WARBE Development Foundation, said in May 2026 that according to Wage Earners' Welfare Board data about 799 to 800 women migrants have come home dead in the past eight years, that in most cases the cause is given as heart attack or illness and sometimes suicide, and that the real cause is not known.
target_section: Women
why_new: A count of women migrants' deaths and the doubt over recorded causes.

claim: According to BMET data cited at the roundtable, more than 10 lakh Bangladeshi women were working abroad in May 2026, though the number of women migrating has fallen in the last few years, and more than 10 lakh 95 thousand women went abroad between 2001 and 2022; RMMRU's programme director said women are about 13.5 percent of total migration.
target_section: Women
why_new: Size of women's migration; the two speakers differ on whether the trend is falling or still rising.

claim: S K Mojibul Haque, director of BNSK, said in May 2026 that most women workers have to work 12 to 14 hours instead of 8.
target_section: Women
why_new: Working hours as reported by a women migrants' organisation.
